> I am building a modular portable computer using recovered Lenovo ThinkPad Edge E545 components. The design includes a custom 3D-printed computer enclosure and three stackable expansion trays, attached with side screws, with rear openings for power and data cables. I previously explored the concept during the warm-up. In this phase, I will verify component measurements, refine the CAD models, design the mounting points and cable routing, and test the assembly.(i used for my warm up project

## Design

### 2026-10-05 – I prepared a preliminary design for the ModuDeck Module Monitor. It uses a Raspberry Pi Pico, three presence switches and three status LEDs to detect which expansion trays are attached. The documentat

**3h**

I prepared a preliminary design for the ModuDeck Module Monitor. It uses a Raspberry Pi Pico, three presence switches and three status LEDs to detect which expansion trays are attached. The documentation includes a system diagram, input circuit, pin map and proposed component placement. A MicroPython firmware draft was also added, with software tests for switch debouncing. The hardware has not been tested, and the KiCad schematic and routed PCB still need to be completed. My next step is to review the connections, select the actual components and develop the PCB in KiCad.

### 2026-10-06 – I explored three concept views for ModuDeck: the computer with three stackable expansion trays, rear cable routing, and a separate enclosure for the Module Monitor. The proposed improvements include c

**3h**

I explored three concept views for ModuDeck: the computer with three stackable expansion trays, rear cable routing, and a separate enclosure for the Module Monitor. The proposed improvements include cable clamps, removable covers and three visible status LEDs. The monitor is intended to detect tray presence using switches and report it to the computer over USB; it will not power the expansion trays. These images are conceptual illustrations, not validated CAD models or photographs of built hardware. The next step is to create and check the KiCad schematic, choose component footprints and develop the PCB layout.

### 2026-10-07 – Today's update documents the preliminary ModuDeck Module Monitor design with three technical drawings prepared with AI assistance. They show the three tray-presence inputs, the status LED connections

**3h**

Today's update documents the preliminary ModuDeck Module Monitor design with three technical drawings prepared with AI assistance. They show the three tray-presence inputs, the status LED connections and USB link, and a proposed integration inside the computer enclosure. Each tray would use a normally-open switch, while the Pico would report its presence over USB. The proposed internal placement keeps the monitor within the PC level, with detachable sensor cables running to the three trays. Component footprints, mounting clearances and cable routing still need verification. These drawings are planning documentation: the KiCad schematic, PCB routing and physical testing remain to be completed.

### 2026-10-09 – With AI assistance, I organised the preliminary Module Monitor design into three planning sheets: a circuit summary, a component list with quantities, and a proposed PCB arrangement. The design uses a

**3h**

With AI assistance, I organised the preliminary Module Monitor design into three planning sheets: a circuit summary, a component list with quantities, and a proposed PCB arrangement. The design uses a Raspberry Pi Pico, three tray-presence switches and three status LEDs. The placement proposal keeps the USB connector accessible and groups each input connector with its resistors. Exact component models, footprints, prices and board dimensions still need verification. These images document preparation for the PCB design; they are not exports from a completed KiCad project. The next steps are to draw the schematic, run ERC, assign footprints, route the board and run DRC before generating manufacturing files.

### 2026-10-11 – This update brings together the preliminary design documentation for the ModuDeck Module Monitor, prepared with AI assistance. The proposed circuit uses a Raspberry Pi Pico to detect three removable t

**6h**

This update brings together the preliminary design documentation for the ModuDeck Module Monitor, prepared with AI assistance. The proposed circuit uses a Raspberry Pi Pico to detect three removable trays through switches and display their status using three LEDs. USB provides power and communication with the computer.
The six drawings cover the input circuits, LED connections, integration inside the computer, schematic preparation, preliminary component quantities and a proposed PCB arrangement. These are planning drawings, not screenshots of a completed KiCad design. The next steps are to create the schematic in KiCad, select the exact components and footprints, route the board and run the electrical and design-rule checks. No physical circuit has been tested yet.
